passages.where: The last of the Ten Commandments forbids coveting the neighbour's house and anything that belongs to him. The site's note says it reaches from acts to the desire that produces them, that no court could enforce it, and that it lays bare the root from which the other offenses grow. The law ends by looking at the heart.

Jesus says that from within the heart come evil thoughts and a list of evils, greed among them, and that these are what defile a person. The site's note says the list puts attitudes beside acts, so that no one who has avoided murder and theft can count himself clean. The plain note says it is easier to worry about what is out there than to look at what is in here.

Confronted after the defeat at Ai, Achan confesses that he saw a cloak, silver and gold among the spoils, coveted them, took them and hid them in his tent. The site's note on the chapter says he took them secretly from the things devoted to the LORD. The verse gives the whole movement of greed in four verbs, from the eye to the hiding place.

King Ahab wants the vineyard next to his palace, and when Naboth will not sell his family's inheritance, Ahab lies on his bed, turns his face away and refuses to eat. The site's note on the chapter tells how Jezebel then arranged false witnesses so that Naboth was killed and Ahab took the land. A king with everything sulked over a vineyard, and wanting became taking.

Elisha refuses the healed Naaman's gifts, and his servant Gehazi decides to run after him and get something for himself. The site's note on the chapter says he secretly takes some of the gifts. A gift of grace freely given was, to Gehazi, a missed opportunity.

Woe to those who add house to house and field to field until no place is left and they live alone in the land. The site's note on the chapter lists this first among six woes, against land-grabbing. Greed in Isaiah does not only harm the neighbour pushed out; it leaves the grasper alone.

Micah pronounces woe on those who plot evil on their beds and at morning take the fields and houses they covet, because the power is in their hands. The site's note on the chapter says these powerful men lie awake plotting how to seize their neighbours' fields and houses. Greed with power behind it becomes injustice.

The Teacher has seen wealth hoarded to the harm of its owner, or lost in a failed venture, and observes that everyone leaves the world as naked as they came. The site's note on the chapter says he shows how the love of money never satisfies and how riches can be hoarded or lost. What greed gathers cannot be carried out.

When Mary pours perfume on Jesus, Judas asks why it was not sold for the poor, and John says he did not care about the poor but was a thief who took from the money bag. The site's note says this is the first time the Gospel gives Judas a character beyond the label of betrayer. The plain note says Judas talked about the poor but loved money, and asks which voice is louder in you.

Paul tells the church to put to death the earthly nature, naming greed among sins of desire and calling it idolatry. The site's plain note asks which of his lists you are more likely to excuse in yourself, and what put to death would mean for one habit you know well. The site's note on Luke 12 says Paul calls it idolatry because it looks to possessions for what only God gives, and calls it the most respectable idol.

misread.taken: Everyone who has will be given more is quoted as if Jesus approved of piling up wealth, or as if riches showed God's favour and more would follow for those who already have plenty.
misread.says: The site's plain note says the parable of the talents is not about making money: it is not a promise that God will make the faithful rich and not a rule about investing, and it cannot be used to say that wealth shows God's favour. It says this saying, which Jesus used before about understanding the kingdom, is not about bank balances: whoever uses what God gives will be given more, and whoever buries it loses even that. In the very next passage, the note adds, Jesus says he is found among the hungry and the poor.

whole: Greed rarely calls itself greed. It calls itself ambition, prudence, deserving a little more, keeping up, not falling behind. It shows in the restless scroll through things to buy, the raise that is spent before it arrives, the comparison with the neighbour's car or the friend's holiday, the inheritance quarrel that splits a family, and in the person who has plenty and still cannot give. It is not only a sin of the rich. A person with very little can be ruled by wanting, and a person with a great deal can hold it loosely.

Scripture traces greed to the heart. The tenth commandment reaches past every act to the desire, and Jesus lists greed among the evils that come from within. The Bible's stories show its movement: Achan saw, coveted, took and hid; Ahab, a king with everything, sulked over a neighbour's vineyard until wanting became taking; Gehazi ran after a gift his master had refused; Judas spoke of the poor and stole from the common purse. The prophets show what it does with power behind it, field joined to field until the grasper lives alone in the land. And Paul names the root when he calls greed idolatry: it looks to things for the security, worth and rest that belong to God, which is why it never says enough. Most of us can find some of this in ourselves if we look honestly.

So the Bible's wisdom is not only to want less but to want rightly. Name the desire before it becomes an act, as the tenth commandment does. Notice where you excuse yourself, as the plain note on Colossians asks. Give on purpose, first and regularly, because an open hand is the opposite of a grasping one. Learn contentment as a practice, since the Teacher says the love of money never satisfies and everyone leaves this world as naked as they came. And remember those who are pushed out by someone else's getting, the Naboths and the neighbours whose fields are taken, because greed is never only private.

The hope Scripture gives is that the heart which wants so much was made for something greater than anything it grasps. The psalmist tells his own soul that if riches increase, do not set your heart on them, because power and loving devotion belong to God. The one who fills that place does not need to be seized or hoarded. He gives, and those who receive him find, often to their surprise, that they can let go of what they were holding.
sit: What do you keep telling yourself you need, and what are you hoping it will give you?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says verse 10 asks a quiet question: what are you leaning your heart on that weighs less than a breath? Pray these lines when you notice the wanting.
